citations.quote: Not to blow up his family's financial stability

arguments.impact: The goal is legitimate, but preserving household stability is an explicit constraint; optimize for a reversible experiment, not a dramatic leap.
arguments.text: My initial position: explore software without quitting the mechanical-engineering job. Keep income and savings protected while testing whether the work and market fit you.

arguments.impact: The lower financial exposure does not make this effortless or guarantee completion.
arguments.text: Self-study while employed is financially safer, but scarce time and burnout risk can make a long plan stall.

citations.quote: Her support is real but qualified.
A decision that violates a genuine floor isn't bold

arguments.impact: Her genuine buy-in and agreed floors should be prerequisites for any plan that materially shifts family time or finances.
arguments.text: Lisa's conditional support and family bandwidth are material—not obstacles to overcome. Set financial, relationship, and time floors together.

citations.quote: Dave hinted at a lead-engineer path.

arguments.impact: A deployed project can test aptitude and create evidence; the internal path is another option, not proof that software is wrong.
arguments.text: Build a polished deployed project grounded in automotive knowledge, and investigate Dave's lead-engineer path in parallel. Compare actual interest and opportunity rather than assuming either route is best.

arguments.impact: Without monthly spending, target salary, time capacity, market evidence, or Lisa's agreed limits, no responsible savings threshold or job-switch date can be calculated.
arguments.text: Assuming you can study without jeopardizing work or family commitments, run a bounded trial: agree with Lisa on weekly hours, a savings floor, and a review date; build and deploy the project; then reassess interest, progress, and employer feedback. Do not quit or pay for a bootcamp until those limits and a realistic budget are established.

criteria.text: Preserve current income during exploration; no recommendation to quit or spend substantial savings absent a quantified household budget and agreed financial floor.
Treat Lisa as a stakeholder: materially affecting family finances or time requires genuine agreement and explicit household limits.
Use a concrete, low-cost test of software aptitude and employability, without promising hiring outcomes.
Compare software with the possible internal career path and probe what success and desired work mean to Mark.

missing_data: Monthly household expenses and emergency savings floor; current savings alone do not establish available runway.
Lisa's explicit agreement on study hours, financial floor, and review/stop rule.
Mark's available weekly study time and a realistic deadline, accounting for full-time work and childcare.
Specific software role, target salary floor, local/employer hiring requirements, and evidence of demand.
Whether Mark seeks software work itself or primarily wants to leave mechanical engineering; what success means at 12 months.
recommendation: Do not resign or commit $14,000 to a bootcamp now. Keep the current job while agreeing with Lisa on household financial and time floors, completing a bare-bones budget, and setting a review date. In a limited trial, build and deploy one useful automotive-domain project and seek specific feedback from software practitioners/employers; in parallel, learn what Dave's lead-engineer path entails. Review whether the work engages you, whether progress is feasible alongside family obligations, and whether real hiring signals justify the next investment. Make no job-exit decision until the budget, agreed stopping rule, and acceptable salary floor are explicit. This preserves optionality but may delay a transition and carries a risk that self-study stalls.
strongest_counterargument: Keeping the job and studying part-time may prolong uncertainty and increase burnout; the dossier says self-study can take 18–24 months and quietly stall. A structured bootcamp could address a discipline bottleneck, and delay has an opportunity cost. But there is no evidence here that discipline is the bottleneck or that tuition improves this household's odds enough to justify spending savings; quantify the budget and test the work first.
